name: Gwahatike
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Price, Dorothy. 1989. Gwahatike Organised Phonology Data. SIL (OPDs include a suprasegmentals/stress section; SIL site returned 403)

new_statements.quote: Stress is inherent in vowel length. In two syllable words stress is allocated in the first syllable. In three syllable words if the second syllable is long, the stress is moved to the second syllable from the first one. In the words that are more than three syllables stress still remains on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Price, Dorothy [data checked by; compiled per the sheet's bibliography by An, Jee-Young]. 1989. Guahatike Organised Phonology Data [header: 'Organised Phonology Data. Gwahatike (Dahating) Language [DAH]. Madang Province']. Ukarumpa: SIL PNG Branch, 5 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42402 (PDF printed 23 Aug 2004).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default initial stress, sensitive to vowel length: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; in trisyllables a long (bimoraic) second vowel attracts the stress to the second syllable, otherwise the first; words of four or more syllables are stressed on the first syllable regardless. The sheet ties stress to vowel length ('inherent in vowel length'), so the pattern is quantity-sensitive with an initial default rather than fixed-initial.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the trisyllable case: a long second syllable takes the stress. No lexical exceptions listed; the sheet gives no stress-marked examples (examples elsewhere mark length with (:) but not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (an SIL OPD 'Suprasegmentals' statement); citation forms, no phrase-level statement. The heading names tone but the sheet says nothing about tone; vowel length is phonemic (short/long pairs listed pp. 2-3).
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD's header reads 'Gwahatike (Dahating) Language [DAH], Madang Province, Trans New Guinea Phylum; Finisterre Stock; Warup Family; Major villages: Umboldi'; the SIL catalogue records it as 'Guahatike' with subject language Gwahatike [dah] = gwah1244 (language level). No dialect is specified; Glottolog lists Dahating as a dialect (gwap1238) but the sheet uses 'Dahating' as an alternate name for the whole language, as does Claassen & McElhanon 1970 (p. 53, wordlist from Wilwilan). Authorship note: the SIL catalogue credits Dorothy Price 1989; the sheet itself says 'Data checked by: Dorothy Price' and its bibliography credits 'An, Jee-Young. 1989. Organized Phonological Data of Guahatike Language' — cite as Price (comp./checker) with An as compiler.

sources.note: p. 4 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress is inherent in vowel length; two-syllable words stressed on the first syllable; in three-syllable words a long second syllable takes the stress; words of more than three syllables keep initial stress. No secondary stress, no tone. Verified against a page render.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 p. 53 treats 'Dahating' (= Gwahatike) as an isolate with a 45-item wordlist from Wilwilan and lexicostatistics only; sec. 6.1 phonology remarks (pp. 66-67, note 11) mention stress only for Rawa (phonemic), Yupna/Wantoat (probably sub-phonemic) and Suroi.
